name: McVittie Mass in an Expanding Universe
description: A point mass in a spatially flat expanding universe, the solution George McVittie found in 1933 for a perfect fluid at rest about the mass. Where a positive cosmological constant drives the late expansion, it holds a black hole whose horizon approaches that of Schwarzschild-de Sitter.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and the scale factor $a(t)$ of the spatially flat universe is dimensionless. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: George McVittie asked in 1933 which metric an observer beside the Sun should assign to a universe whose nebulae recede [mcvittie1933]. Georges Lemaître had proposed one in 1931, and McVittie judged that it made the pressure of the surrounding matter negative wherever its density is positive [lemaitre1931expanding, mcvittie1933]. A second, which he had found with William McCrea, had the matter of the universe flowing toward the Sun "with a high velocity which is certainly not observed" [mccrea1930, mccrea1931, mcvittie1933]. McVittie required that the matter flow neither toward the mass nor away from it and that its pressure be isotropic, and solved Einstein's equations for $$ds^2 = -\left(\frac{1 - \dfrac{r_s}{4ar}}{1 + \dfrac{r_s}{4ar}}\right)^2c^2dt^2 + a^2\left(1 + \frac{r_s}{4ar}\right)^4\left(dr^2 + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\right),$$ with $a(t)$ the scale factor of a spatially flat universe [mcvittie1933]. At $r_s = 0$ it is that universe, and at constant $a$ it is Schwarzschild's metric in isotropic coordinates [kaloper2010].¶An observer who measures distance from the mass at the instant $t_1$ uses $r_1 = a(t_1)r$, and in that coordinate McVittie's metric near the mass is Schwarzschild's static field with the same mass at every $t_1$ [mcvittie1933]. For a planet on a slow orbit of short period he concluded that "the orbit of the planet and the mass of the central particle remain fixed, whilst the system of the nebulæ increases in size" [mcvittie1933]. He showed that for a cosmological constant $\lambda \le 0$, with a density and a pressure that cannot be negative, the expansion decelerates at every instant, and concluded that the observer "would necessarily take $\lambda$ to be a positive constant" [mcvittie1933]. Roshina Nandra, Anthony Lasenby, and Michael Hobson derived the metric anew in 2012 in a radial coordinate that is not comoving, and worked out its geodesic equations [nandra2012]. In the Newtonian limit they found an inward force on a test particle proportional to the inverse square of the radius and a cosmological force proportional to the radius, directed outward when the expansion accelerates and inward when it decelerates [nandra2012].¶Albert Einstein and Ernst Straus matched the two geometries in 1945 by cutting a ball out of a universe of dust and filling it with Schwarzschild's solution for the mass removed [einstein1945, carrera2010]. Inside that vacuole the geometry is exactly Schwarzschild's, so a system within it does not feel the expansion outside [carrera2010]. McVittie's fluid fills the space down to the mass with a density $\rho$ that is uniform on each surface of constant $t$, $8\pi G\rho = 3H^2$ with the Hubble rate $H = (da/dt)/a$ [kaloper2010]. Its pressure is $$\frac{8\pi G p}{c^2} = -3H^2 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{1 - r_s/R}}\frac{dH}{dt},$$ where $R = ar\left(1 + r_s/4ar\right)^2$ is the areal radius, and its gradient balances the attraction of the mass, so the mass accretes nothing [kaloper2010]. Where $dH/dt \neq 0$ the pressure and the Ricci scalar diverge on the sphere $R = r_s$, a curvature singularity, and where $H$ is constant the metric is that of Schwarzschild-de Sitter [kaloper2010, carrera2010].¶Brien Nolan gave criteria in 1998 for a spacetime to represent a point mass in a Robertson-Walker universe, built on Stephen Hawking's quasilocal mass, and showed that McVittie's spatially flat solution meets them [nolan1998]. He found that the singular surface $R = r_s$ is spacelike [nolan1998]. Nemanja Kaloper, Matthew Kleban, and Damien Martin studied in 2010 a universe of fluid and a positive cosmological constant, in which $H$ falls to a constant $H_0 > 0$ [kaloper2010]. Of the singular surface they wrote that it "lies in the causal past of all spacetime points in the patch of the metric we are studying, so we refer to it as the big bang" [kaloper2010]. Ingoing light rays reach the surface $R = r_-$, $t = \infty$ at a finite affine parameter, where $r_-$ is the smaller positive root of $1 - r_s/R - H_0^2R^2/c^2 = 0$ [kaloper2010]. Every curvature invariant there takes its value on the horizon of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole of the same $r_s$ and $H_0$, so the surface is a regular black hole horizon [kaloper2010].¶Kayll Lake and Majd Abdelqader took $H = H_0\coth(3H_0t/2)$ in 2011, the expansion of a universe of dust and a cosmological constant, and integrated the radial null geodesics numerically to build the conformal diagram [lake2011]. They found that the boundary contains the bifurcation sphere of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime, so that a white hole horizon and a black hole horizon both bound McVittie's solution [lake2011]. The null and weak energy conditions hold throughout it [lake2011]. Valerio Faraoni, Andres Zambrano Moreno, and Roshina Nandra showed in 2012 that in a universe dominated by dust no black hole exists at early times, since its apparent horizon would be larger than the cosmological one [faraoni2012]. Alan da Silva, Michele Fontanini, and Daniel Guariento proved a theorem in 2013 that tells from the scale factor whether a black hole alone or a black hole and a white hole bound the spacetime [dasilva2013].

related.text: McVittie's metric with the expansion stopped. At constant $a$ it is Schwarzschild's in isotropic coordinates [kaloper2010].
McVittie's metric with the mass removed, $r_s = 0$, the spatially flat Friedmann universe with the same $a(t)$ [kaloper2010].
McVittie's universe expanding at a steady rate, with $H$ constant [kaloper2010, carrera2010].

coordinates.name: Isotropic Comoving

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$, $\dot{a} > 0$) of the spatially flat universe

coordinates.convention: We use McVittie's cosmic time $t$ and a comoving isotropic radius $r$, a length, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot on the scale factor is $\dot{a} = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{t} + \dfrac{8r\,r_s\,\dot{a}}{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{16a\,r_s}{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}\dot{t}\dot{r} + \dfrac{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)^5\,\dot{a}}{256a^3\,r^4\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)^5\,\dot{a}}{256a^3\,r^2\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)^5\,\dot{a}\sin^2\theta}{256a^3\,r^2\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{r} + \dfrac{2048a^3\,r^4\,r_s\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)}{\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)^7}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{2\left(4a\,r - r_s\right)\dot{a}}{a\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)}\dot{t}\dot{r} - \dfrac{2r_s}{r\left(4a\,r + r_s\right)}\dot{r}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(r_s - 4a\,r\right)}{4a\,r + r_s}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{r\left(r_s - 4a\,r\right)\sin^2\theta}{4a\,r + r_s}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Areal Radius
coordinates.convention: We use the cosmic time $t$ and the areal radius $R = ar\left(1 + r_s/4ar\right)^2$, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot on the Hubble rate is $\dot{H} = dH/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

nonzero.value: \dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^2\left(R - r_s\right)^2}
-\dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^2\left(R - r_s\right)^2}

\dfrac{c^4\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)^2 + c^2\,H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)\left(R - 2r_s\right) - H^4\,R^6\left(R - r_s\right) + c^3\,R^{7/2}\left(R - r_s\right)^{3/2}\dot{H} - c\,H^2\,R^{13/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H}}{c^4\,R^4\left(R - r_s\right)}

-\dfrac{c^4\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)^2 + c^2\,H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)\left(R - 2r_s\right) - H^4\,R^6\left(R - r_s\right) + c^3\,R^{7/2}\left(R - r_s\right)^{3/2}\dot{H} - c\,H^2\,R^{13/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H}}{c^4\,R^4\left(R - r_s\right)}
-\dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)}
\dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)}
\dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)}
-\dfrac{c\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H} + H^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^2\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right)}
\dfrac{3c^2\,H^2\left(R - r_s\right)^2 - 3H^4\,R^3\left(R - r_s\right) + c^3\,\sqrt{R}\left(R - r_s\right)^{3/2}\dot{H} - 3c\,H^2\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H}}{c^4\,R\left(R - r_s\right)}

geodesics: \ddot{t} + \dfrac{H\left(2H^2\,R^3 - c^2\,r_s\right)}{2c^3\,\sqrt{R}\sqrt{R - r_s}}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{c^2\,r_s - 2H^2\,R^3}{c^2\,R\left(R - r_s\right)}\dot{t}\dot{R} + \dfrac{H\,R^{3/2}}{c\left(R - r_s\right)^{3/2}}\dot{R}^2 + \dfrac{H\,R^{5/2}}{c\,\sqrt{R - r_s}}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{H\,R^{5/2}\sin^2\theta}{c\,\sqrt{R - r_s}}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{R} + \dfrac{c^4\,r_s\left(R - r_s\right) - c^2\,H^2\,R^3\left(2R - r_s\right) + 2H^4\,R^6 - 2c^3\,R^{7/2}\sqrt{R - r_s}\dot{H}}{2c^4\,R^3}\dot{t}^2 + \dfrac{H\left(c^2\,r_s - 2H^2\,R^3\right)}{c^3\,\sqrt{R}\sqrt{R - r_s}}\dot{t}\dot{R} + \dfrac{2H^2\,R^3 - c^2\,r_s}{2c^2\,R\left(R - r_s\right)}\dot{R}^2 + \dfrac{H^2\,R^3 - c^2\left(R - r_s\right)}{c^2}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{\left(H^2\,R^3 - c^2\left(R - r_s\right)\right)\sin^2\theta}{c^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
